scenes.title: Cold open
narration: Forbidden from using drums, enslaved people in the American South transformed their own bodies into percussion instruments to preserve the sacred rhythms of the Kongo.
This is Juba dance. 18th-19th century.
on_screen: Title card: Juba dance · United States · 18th-19th century

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Juba dance was brought by enslaved peoples from the Kongo to Charleston, South Carolina, as early as the 18th century.
It originated from the Kikongo word 'diuba,' meaning to beat the sun or time, and was originally a sacred step dance called giouba.
On American plantations, it became a vital means of preserving African identity when traditional rhythm instruments were banned by slaveholders who feared secret codes hidden in drumming.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: In its original context, Juba was a tool for resilience and communication, used to relay information similarly to talking drums.
It also carried spiritual significance related to the Kongo religion's circle of life.
The lyrics often contained social commentary on the conditions of slavery, such as the rhyme 'You sift the meal and ya gimme the husk,' which highlighted the exploitation of enslaved labor.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance involves a complex series of body percussion techniques including stomping the feet and slapping or patting the arms, legs, chest, and cheeks.
It was often used to keep time for other dances during a walkaround.
Watch for Long Dog Scratch, Blow That Candle Out.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Circle formation simulating the circle of life; used in walkarounds
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Because drums were prohibited, the body itself serves as the primary instrument.
The music is defined by complex rhythmic patterns created through clapping and patting.
Listen for the Body percussion, Feet, Hands, Chest.

A layered percussive soundscape created entirely by the human body, featuring deep thuds from chest-patting, sharp cracks from hand-claps, and rhythmic shuffling or stomping of the feet, often overlaid with rhythmic chanting.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Originally performed in the informal setting of plantation gatherings and slave quarters, the dance required no specific costume other than the everyday attire of the enslaved.
In later 19th-century public performances and minstrel shows, it was performed on stages.

Today, it is seen in university settings during step-shows and in professional dance theaters, often performed in contemporary athletic or performance wear that allows for unrestricted movement and clear percussive sound.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The most famous Juba dancer was William Henry Lane, known as Master Juba, who was one of the first Black performers in the United States to achieve international fame.
In the realm of music, composer Florence Price utilized Juba rhythms in her symphonies, and Bo Diddley popularized the 'Hambone' rhythm in rock and roll.
The dance was practiced across the American South, the Caribbean (where it was known as Djouba in Haiti), and Dutch Guiana (Suriname).
Juba is a direct ancestor of modern tap dance and has heavily influenced American stepping.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Juba dance is influence of Tap dance: Juba's popularization by Master Juba played a significant role in the development of tap.
Juba dance is variant of Stepping: Modern African American step-shows are a contemporary expression of Juba's rhythmic legacy.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Originally a sacred step dance related to the movement of the sun in traditional Kongo religion; it simulates the circle of life and ancestral spirituality.
